The French grunt, Haemulon flavolineatum, is a common reef fish whose life history traits have been characterized from populations across the Caribbean. Field surveys consistently record that most adults fall well short of this ceiling, with the median individual measuring considerably less, but the large maximum value underscores the species’ potential when resources are abundant and mortality is low.

The ultimate wet weight of 364 grams [Wwi = 364 grams] for Haemulon flavolineatum is reached through a growth trajectory that typically spans several years and is characterized by an initial rapid phase followed by a plateau as the fish approaches its asymptotic body size. The asymptotic mass thus places the French grunt in a mid-tier trophic role, capable of exploiting a broad range of benthic invertebrate prey but still vulnerable to larger piscivores.

The oldest documented individuals consistently come from protected areas with low fishing pressure, implying that anthropogenic mortality is a primary constraint on realized lifespan in exploited populations. From a physiological standpoint, achieving this age requires efficient repair mechanisms and a robust immune system capable of handling chronic parasite loads common in reef environments. The combination of a long lifespan with a relatively low daily reproductive rate aligns with a bet-hedging strategy, where the risk of reproductive failure in any given year is offset by the opportunity to spawn repeatedly across multiple breeding seasons.
